A student-made guide for Queens College Political Science majors headed to graduate school or law school: paid research programs, internships, fellowships, deadlines and sample résumés, with every program linked to its official page.

Choose a path

  • Graduate school PhD, predoc, MPP, MPA and MA: funded PhDs, paid research jobs and policy master's degrees, with a timeline for each year of college.
  • Law school The JD: the LSAT and fee waivers, pre-law programs, legal internships and gap years.

How it works

Pick your path, then a degree. Each degree page explains the degree, gives a timeline for each year of college, and lists the programs that prepare you for it, sorted by next deadline. The Guides pages cover professors, methods, applying and résumés.

  • Good programs pay you. Almost everything here is free and comes with a stipend, housing, or both.
  • Deadlines move every year. Confirm on the official page before you plan around a date.
  • Ask for help. Professors, QC Pre-Law Advising and the Office of Honors and Scholarships are here to help you apply.

Choosing a graduate degree

A political science degree leads to several kinds of graduate programs. Open one to see what it is and what it takes. Not sure yet? Most of the programs on this site exist to help you find out.

  • PhD Research and teaching. Funded, 5–6 years
  • Predoc A paid research job before a PhD. Any major, 1–2 years
  • MPP Design and evaluate policy. About 2 years
  • MPA Run public and nonprofit organizations. 1–2 years
  • MA Graduate study and methods, no PhD required. 1–2 years
  • Guides Professors, methods, applying, scholarships and job search tools

Hello! I made this site because, as an undergrad, I didn't know about all the opportunities I had. It's based on my own experience, so it won't match everyone's. Questions or comments? Email me at mohamed.aljahmi@qc.cuny.edu. I'm always happy to help and can point you to the right resources on campus.

What a PhD is

Original research and teaching. A PhD prepares you to be a professor, or to do research at think tanks, in government and in tech. Political science PhD programs pay you.

  • Length: 5–6 years
  • Who pays: The school: tuition plus a stipend. 2026–27: Princeton $52,680, Duke $43,775, CUNY Graduate Center $31,141
  • Pick it if: You want answering questions with data or theory to be your career
  • Apply: Fall of senior year or later. Most deadlines fall Dec 1–17; Columbia's is Nov 25. See Applying

A political science PhD can also lead to data science. PhD students train in statistics, causal inference, survey design and coding, and some go straight into industry. Michigan's placement records include a research scientist on Meta's demography and survey science team, a director of data science at Civiqs and a lead data scientist at Cox Automotive. MIT's include a data scientist at NORC. Choosing methodology as a minor field keeps that door open.

A master's is not required for a PhD. Most political science PhD students are admitted straight from a BA or after a paid research job. A paid year or two first is normal; the standard route is a predoc, a full-time research assistant job.

Where to look. predoc.org is the main job board; filter by political economy or public policy. Listings go stale, so confirm on the lab's own page. For a pay benchmark, Stanford's SIEPR economics predoc posted $64,260 a year.

PhDs beyond political science

CUNY Graduate Center

Doctoral programs across the social sciences

Anthropology, Criminal Justice, Economics, Educational Psychology, Political Science, Psychology, Sociology, Linguistics and Urban Education. The GC also offers an M.S. in Quantitative Methods in the Social Sciences and a Demography Certificate.

NYU PhD in Statistics and Computational Social Science

NYU Steinhardt · due Dec 1

Combines statistics, computation and social science on problems in public health, education and criminal justice. Graduates go into academia, nonprofits, government and industry.

Michigan PhD in Information

School of Information · due Dec 1 · no GRE

Computational social science is one of its research areas, and some of its faculty also work with Michigan's Center for Political Studies. Funded with tuition, a stipend and health insurance for 12 months a year.

Find your subfield

You don't have to be a "methods person" to get a political science PhD. You apply to study one subfield, only some subfields are math-heavy, and most programs teach statistics from the start.

The five core subfields

American politics

Math: Mixed · often quantitative

Also called American government and politics

U.S. institutions such as Congress, the presidency and the courts, plus elections, public opinion and political behavior.

  • Look for: No special prerequisites are listed. Expect statistics: Harvard's math prefresher notes it is hard to take American politics courses without meeting statistical or game-theoretic models

Comparative politics

Math: Mixed · qualitative and quantitative

Compares politics across countries and regions: democracy, development, civil war, institutions and identity.

  • Look for: A foreign language and knowledge of a region. Rutgers tests majors in the language they need, and Michigan advises starting languages before graduate school
  • Research: Berkeley PhD students usually spend at least a year doing fieldwork

International relations

Math: Mixed · depends on approach

Also called international relations and world politics

War and security, trade, international law and organizations, and why countries cooperate or fight.

  • Look for: Methods vary: historical, statistical and game-theoretic work all appear. No IR-specific prerequisites are listed

Political theory

Math: Light · little math

Also called political thought, or normative political theory and philosophy

Ideas of justice, legitimacy, democracy and power, read through the history of political thought and contemporary philosophy.

  • Look for: Reading in philosophy, history or classics, and often a foreign language: UVA requires one for theory majors
  • Methods: Duke's methods requirements don't apply to theory students, Harvard lets them skip its methods course, and Berkeley weighs math less for theory applicants

Methodology and formal theory

Math: Heavy · real math

Also called research methods, quantitative methodology, or formal and quantitative analysis

Methodologists build the statistical and research-design tools other political scientists use. Formal theorists use game-theory models of strategic choices.

  • Look for: Math and statistics. Duke's methodology field expects competency in both, and Michigan asks methods majors for math coursework
  • Tip: Many students take methods as a minor next to a substantive subfield

You don't have to arrive methods-heavy

  • Math camps. Harvard, Stanford, Michigan, Princeton and UC San Diego run summer math courses for incoming PhD students. At Harvard, almost every first-year student takes it.
  • Methods from scratch. Stanford says you don't need advanced quantitative courses to be admitted, and its first-year sequence assumes no background in statistics or advanced math.
  • Language or methods. At the CUNY Graduate Center, UCLA, Yale and Columbia, a research-tools requirement can be met with a foreign language or with methods courses.
  • Your topic can change. Michigan notes that students often change focus once coursework starts. The statement of purpose is not a contract.

Be honest with yourself about math. Quantitative skills still count. Most top programs require the GRE again, and Stanford reports admitted students typically score 163 or higher on the quantitative section. Stanford also requires two methods courses of every PhD student. Taking PSCI 200 and an intro statistics course, such as PSYCH 107 or DATA 205, helps whichever subfield you choose.

Other fields at some schools

Some departments add fields beyond the core five. Check whether a field can be your main field or only a minor.

  • Public policy. CUNY Graduate Center (Public Policy, with areas like health, education, housing and urban development), UC Berkeley (Public Policy & Organization), UT Austin, Texas A&M (Public Policy / Public Administration), Syracuse (public administration and policy) and Michigan (a student-designed Public Policy and Administration minor).
  • Law and courts. Princeton and Rutgers (Public Law), Michigan (Law, Courts, and Politics), UC Berkeley (Public Law & Jurisprudence), Washington and UT Austin, which also has a combined JD/PhD.
  • Race, ethnicity and gender. UCLA (Race, Ethnicity & Politics), Rutgers (Women and Politics), UC Berkeley, Washington and Ohio State (Race, Ethnicity, and Gender).
  • Political psychology and behavior. Stony Brook, Ohio State and Minnesota (as a minor).
  • Political economy and formal theory. Rochester (formal political theory; every student takes it or methodology), Yale, NYU and UChicago, which runs a separate Political Economy PhD with its public policy school. Expect heavy math.
  • Organized by theme. Duke has no American, comparative or international relations fields. Its six fields are Political Behavior & Identities, Political Institutions, Political Economy, Security, Peace & Conflict, Political Methodology, and Normative Political Theory & Philosophy.

PhD timeline

Junior year is the busiest stretch: RBSI, PPIA, MIT, Leadership Alliance, SROP and Truman all open or close between October and February.

Programs that prepare you for a PhD. Most summer research programs open between late September and early November and close between mid-January and mid-February.

What a predoc is

A predoc is a full-time, paid research job with a professor or research center, usually for one or two years before a PhD. You clean data, run analyses and see how research gets made. Economics departments hire the most predocs, but political science, sociology and public policy centers hire them too, and you don't need to major in economics.

  • Length: 1–2 years, usually starting in July
  • Pay: Posted salaries run about $59,500 to $69,300 a year (Stanford GSB, the Stanford King Center, SIEPR and MIT); Stanford IRiSS pays $32.45 an hour
  • Any major: Yale ISPS "very strongly encourage[s]" applicants who didn't major in political science, Opportunity Insights says applicants "need not be Economics majors," and the Stanford King Center welcomes "all disciplines"
  • When to apply: The fall of senior year. Many economics predocs close between August and October (in 2026: Opportunity Insights Oct 1, SIEPR Oct 8, Stanford GSB Oct 16; Yale's Tobin Center opens its rolling application Oct 5). Political science ones, such as Yale ISPS and Stanford IRiSS, hire on a rolling basis or in spring
  • Where to look: predoc.org, filtered by field, and the research centers in the list below

What postings ask for

Twelve official predoc postings from September 2026, across economics, political science and public policy, ask for much the same things. Here is how often each came up, and how to build it at Queens College.

None of the twelve set a minimum GPA, but several ask for it, and SIEPR looks for "high grades in quantitative courses." One catch for economics: MATH 231 requires MATH 141 or MATH 151, not the social-science calculus (MATH 131), and ECON 202 (intermediate microeconomics) requires MATH 131 or the equivalent. If you might apply to economics predocs, choose the MATH 141 or MATH 151 track.

Consider an economics minor. Most predocs are in economics, and economics coursework helps you qualify. That doesn't mean you have to do an economics PhD: a predoc is strong research training in general, and some are in finance and behavioral research. Stanford GSB's Research Fellows, for example, work across finance, organizational behavior and political economics. See the economics minor.

Predoc timeline

The key date is the summer before senior year: that's when your writing sample should be done, because many postings close in early fall.

The writing sample

Have an empirical paper finished by the summer before your senior year. It doesn't have to be long: 12 to 15 pages is appropriate. Several postings ask for an excerpt of about 5 pages, so know which section you would send.

  • What makes it empirical. A clear question, real data, a method (at least a regression), results in tables or figures, and an honest section on limitations.
  • Where it can come from. A paper for a writing-intensive seminar, DATA 334, ECON 390 or a chapter of your honors thesis. Ask the professor to read a draft.
  • Data you can use. ICPSR (Queens College is a member), the American National Election Studies, the Cooperative Election Study, IPUMS census and survey data, and NYC Open Data.
  • Write it yourself. A Harvard Kennedy School posting asked for a single-authored sample, and MIT Blueprint Labs says code samples must be "no more than 50% AI-assisted." Use AI as a proofreader at most (see Statements, help and AI).
  • Keep a code sample too. Seven of the twelve postings ask for a code sample or a data task. Keep the R, Stata or Python script behind your paper clean and commented.

What an MPP is

A Master of Public Policy teaches you to analyze and evaluate policy with economics and statistics. It is faster than a PhD, but you usually pay for it.

  • Length: About 2 years
  • Cost: You usually pay. Some schools fund everyone: Princeton SPIA's MPA, a policy degree, covers full tuition for every student
  • At CUNY: Baruch's Marxe School starts an MPP in fall 2027: evening classes, in person and hybrid, 36–39 credits, about 2 years full-time. Tuition is $545 a credit for New York residents, pending CUNY Board approval
  • Pick it if: You want to design policy or judge whether programs work
  • Prepare: Take economics and statistics. For a future MPP or MPA student, the most valuable program is the PPIA Junior Summer Institute

MPP or MPA? Schools use the two labels loosely, so read each program's courses, not just its name. An MPP leans on analysis; an MPA leans on management.

MPP timeline

Junior year is the busiest stretch for policy students: PPIA, the Albany session internships, congressional internships and Truman all close between October and February.

Programs that prepare you for an MPP: policy internships, summer institutes and fellowships.

What an MPA is

A Master of Public Administration teaches you to manage public and nonprofit organizations: budgets, operations and people. CUNY's MPA programs cost far less than private ones.

  • Length: 1–2 years
  • Cost: Baruch Marxe and John Jay charge NY residents $6,375 a semester full-time; Columbia SIPA tuition is $74,220 a year
  • Pick it if: You want to run programs, agencies or nonprofits
  • Prepare: City, state and nonprofit internships, then fellowships like Coro and the CUNY Civil Service Pathways Fellowship

MPA timeline

Future MPA students build a record of public service: city, state and nonprofit work, then a fellowship or a city job.

Opportunities

Programs that prepare you for an MPA: city, state, nonprofit and congressional internships, and fellowships after college.

Sorted by next deadline. Dates are this cycle's where posted; otherwise they are last cycle's, which are usually close. Confirm on the official page.

What an MA is

A master's in political science gives you graduate-level political science and methods without committing to a PhD. It helps if your record needs strengthening first. A master's in methods or data is another route.

  • Length: 1–2 years
  • CUNY: Graduate Center (30 credits, master's thesis); Brooklyn College (30 credits, evening and online); City College offers a Master of International Affairs instead
  • Private: UChicago MAPSS (one year; 73% of graduates who applied to PhDs got funded offers) and Columbia cost far more
  • Methods or data: QC's own Data Analytics programs lead to an MA, with a faster 4+1 route for sociology majors. The Columbia SPS CUNY Fellowship fully funds some Columbia master's for CUNY students
  • Pick it if: You need more methods before a PhD, or want a data career now

MA timeline

An MA works as a bridge to a PhD or a data career. The QC route is the 4+1, which needs a sociology major and a 3.5 GPA by junior spring.

Opportunities

Programs that fit an MA: research programs, data training and funded master’s options.

Sorted by next deadline. Dates are this cycle's where posted; otherwise they are last cycle's, which are usually close. Confirm on the official page.

The MA prepares graduates for market research, program evaluation, public opinion, public health and applied social research jobs.

Start here

This path covers funded PhDs and policy master's for any Queens College Political Science major who is even curious about graduate school. You don't need to be sure yet. Most of these programs exist to help you find out.

Three ground rules

  • Good research programs pay you. Almost everything here is free and comes with a stipend, housing, or both. Be skeptical of programs that charge you to "do research."
  • Deadlines move every year. Confirm on the official page before you plan around a date.
  • Apply to more than one. These programs are competitive, and a rejection says little about you.
  • Take the methods courses early. PSCI 200 (Research Skills) and an intro statistics course such as PSYCH 107 or DATA 205. Either one also counts toward the Data Analytics minor.
  • Ask for research assistant work. No office posts it. Pick one or two professors whose work you understand, and email what you read, what skill you bring and how many hours you have.

Get credit for it. QC's political science internship courses give credit for urban politics, law and advocacy, and international politics placements. CUNY's Rogowsky Internship Program places juniors and seniors in government for 3–12 credits.

Undocumented or an international student? Emory SOAR says it accepts undocumented and international students. MIT MSRP accepts international students with a visa and work authorization. RBSI, MIT and Michigan also take DACA recipients.

Talk to your professors

Your research doesn't have to be political science. Methods travel across fields, and CUNY faculty in many departments need student help with surveys, data, experiments, fieldwork and archives.

What research looks like next door

  • Sociology. Surveys and interviews on inequality, immigration, work and neighborhoods. Home of QC's data analytics program.
  • Economics. Labor markets and policy evaluation, often with large administrative datasets and causal inference.
  • Psychology. Experiments on attitudes, prejudice and decision-making, the base of political psychology.
  • Urban studies. Housing, transit, policing and city budgets, often with NYC open data.
  • Anthropology and history. Fieldwork, oral histories and archives.
  • Linguistics. Text as data, and language and identity (see Pair your major).

Going to office hours

Office hours are not only for grade questions. Professors expect students to come in and ask for advice, and most of the opportunities on this site started with a conversation like that.

  • Go to office hours or email to ask for 15 minutes. It's normal, even if you've never taken their class.
  • Ask for advice, not a favor: "What would you do in my position?" "Which classes or programs should I look at?" "Who else should I talk to?"
  • Ask about their research, and read one of their papers first.
  • Look outside your department. Sociology, economics, psychology and urban studies faculty take political science students too.
  • Follow up. Send a thank-you, then tell them what you did with their advice. That is how a professor becomes a recommender.

Sample email

Subject: Advice on research opportunities, [Your name], [major]

Dear Professor [Last name],

I'm a [year] majoring in [major] at Queens College. I read your [paper or project] on [topic], and I'm interested in [one sentence on why].

I'm hoping to get research experience before applying to [PhD or master's programs]. Could I come to your office hours on [day] to ask for advice on next steps? If you ever need help on a project, I can offer [a skill, e.g., R or survey coding] for [number] hours a week.

Thank you,
[Full name]

Pair your major

Take a broad range of courses early. Trying history, philosophy, economics or urban studies is how you find the questions you actually want to study, and a second field can make you a stronger applicant.

Theory, history and cities

Philosophy

Minor (18 credits) or second major

Arguments about justice, rights and legitimacy, the core of political theory. The minor includes two history-of-philosophy courses (PHIL 140–148). Best for students drawn to political theory.

History

Minor or second major

Primary sources, archives and long-run change. Useful for political theory, comparative politics and the history of American institutions.

Urban Studies

Major, or a BA and MA in five years

City politics, housing, policing and budgets, often with NYC data. The Accelerated MA pairs a BA in Urban Studies with an MA in Urban Affairs in five years, and up to 12 graduate credits count toward both. It needs a 3.0 GPA overall and in the major; majors in other social sciences are considered case by case. Apply at about 45–75 credits. Best for city government and MPA programs.

Sociology

Double major

Survey research and theory; home of Data Analytics. It unlocks the 4+1 BA/MA in data analytics and Mellon Mays, neither of which takes political science alone.

Data, economics and business

A quantitative credential helps for policy, campaign, government and research jobs. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects data scientist jobs to grow 35% from 2025 to 2035 (BLS).

Data Analytics

Minor (21 credits), in Sociology

The easiest add-on for most political science majors, built for students with no background. Courses: DATA 205 (or PSYCH 107 or ECON 249), 212W, 235, 306, 333 and 334 (list). DATA 205, 306 and 333 teach R. Best for analyst and research assistant jobs, predocs and MPP programs.

Math: Data Science and Statistics

BA, as a second major

Statistics, programming and modeling. Best for methods-heavy PhDs and data science jobs.

Economics

Major or minor

Policy analysis and econometrics. Best for MPPs, economics predocs and think tanks. For more advanced methods, the Quantitative Economics BS adds calculus, linear algebra, advanced econometrics and scientific computing, and is a STEM major.

Computer Science

Minors

Also Computer Information Technology. Best for computational social science and tech policy.

Text as data

Courses, a minor or a BS in Linguistics and Communication Disorders

Want to analyze speeches, bills or social media posts with code? The department teaches LCD 151 and 251, Methods in Computational Linguistics I and II. Go further with the minor (built for CS and linguistics majors; 33 credits for other majors) or the BS in Computational Linguistics.

Business and Liberal Arts (BALA)

Honors minor (21 credits), open to all majors

Business concepts, communication and analytical decision-making. Best for consulting, government management and MPA programs.

Skills employers look for, whatever you pair it with

  • A statistical language. R or Python, plus Excel. SQL if you want data jobs.
  • Survey and research design. Writing a questionnaire, sampling, reading a regression table.
  • Short-form writing. Policy memos and one-page briefs, not only seminar papers.
  • Proof. A GitHub page with one or two finished projects. See the samples.

Methods and skills

Queens College already teaches solid research methods in PSCI 200 and in intro statistics courses like PSYCH 107 and DATA 205. Several teach R, including DATA 205, DATA 306, DATA 333 and Professor Earl Asberry's section of PSCI 200. If you want advanced training, the funded summer research programs like RBSI and MIT MSRP teach graduate-level methods. They are just as good as a summer internship, if not better, and some pay more. Outside class, you already have free access to LinkedIn Learning.

Free self-study, in order

  1. Khan Academy, Statistics and probability. A free online course with short videos and practice problems. Start here if you have never taken statistics.
  2. OpenIntro Statistics. Probability, inference and regression from scratch (free PDF).
  3. R for Data Science. Cleaning, plotting and summarizing data in R.
  4. MIT 17.801, Political Science Scope and Methods. How political scientists design research.
  5. Blackwell, A User's Guide to Statistical Inference and Regression. Regression, done carefully. Read it once you have learned the basics of statistics.
  6. Research Design in the Social Sciences and Causal Inference: The Remix. Causal inference, once regression feels comfortable.

Learning outside class

LinkedIn Learning

Free through QC

Video courses in Excel, SQL, Python, R, Tableau, public speaking and writing. Go to linkedin.com/learning, click Sign in, and use your CUNY Login (your CUNYfirst username and password). Add finished certificates to your LinkedIn profile.

ICPSR Summer Program

Michigan and online · 2027 sessions June 14–July 9 and July 6–30 (tentative)

Open to undergrads. 2026 general session: $2,725 at member schools, $4,975 otherwise. Queens College is an ICPSR member, so you get the member rate. Registration for 2027 opens in February. Scholarships reopen December 2026.

Essex Summer School

UK · June 28–Aug 13, 2027

Data analysis courses charged per course. Confirm undergraduate eligibility with the school.

Put what you build on GitHub. A clean replication of a published table in R is a strong line on a PhD or predoc application.

Notes from RBSI

First-hand notes are on the way. Advice from a QC student in the 2026 Ralph Bunche Summer Institute cohort at Duke: applying, the five weeks, the recruitment fair, and what came after.

Statements, help and AI

Pick programs that fit, and get help with your statement. Read what each program focuses on and make sure it matches what you want to study. Then ask your professors and Rebecca Baron, QC's Advisor for Scholarships and Fellowships in the Office of Honors and Scholarships, to help with your statements of purpose. They are here to help. Don't lose out on an opportunity because you were scared to ask. You're in college to learn, so learn.

Don't let AI write your application. AI is useful for some tasks, like building this website. But professors read the applications to these programs, and they will know if AI wrote yours. Use it as a proofreader instead: give it the prompt and your own draft, and ask where you could improve or show more of yourself. It's a machine, and it doesn't know you better than you know yourself. Before you submit, have peers and professors read your writing too.

Applying

Political science PhD applications are due from late November to December 17 for fall entry (Columbia's is Nov 25), and the APSA Diversity Fellowship closes earlier, on October 25, 2026.

Application fees ($75–$125 each) and who waives them

Program not on the list? Email the department's graduate coordinator and ask anyway, in October rather than the week of the deadline.

The GRE is back at most top programs

  • Required for fall 2027. Harvard (Government), Princeton, Stanford, Yale, Duke, Berkeley, Columbia, MIT, UChicago, UCLA.
  • Not required. Michigan, Wisconsin, Northwestern, CUNY Graduate Center.
  • Plan. Check each program page, and test by early fall of senior year.

The rest of the file

  • Letters (usually 3). From faculty who have seen your research or writing. Ask 6–8 weeks ahead: see Recommendation letters.
  • Statement of purpose. Lead with the question you want to study, show your preparation, and name 2–3 faculty per school whose work fits.
  • Writing sample. Your best research paper, often a seminar paper or thesis chapter, cut to the page limit and revised with a professor.
  • Where to apply. Fit with faculty matters more than rank. Look for people whose recent papers you would want to have written.

Recommendation letters

Most programs ask for two or three letters. PhD programs want them from professors. For law school, MPA and MPP programs and jobs, a supervisor from a job or internship can write one too.

Not close with any professors or employers?

Most students aren't at first. Professors write letters all the time, and they say yes when you make it easy for them.

  • Pick a class you did well in, ideally one where you got a B or above and participated.
  • Ask to meet. Look up their office hours, or email to ask when you could meet on Zoom.
  • Ask 6–8 weeks before the deadline, not the week of.
  • Send everything in one email: your résumé, a draft of your statement and your list of programs with deadlines.
  • Remind and thank. Send a short reminder a week before the deadline, and tell them where you got in.

Sample email

Subject: Letter of recommendation for [program], [Your name]

Dear Professor [Last name],

I took your [course number and name] in [semester], and I especially enjoyed [a topic or reading from the class]. I'm interested in [your interest], and I'm applying to [program or job], due [date].

Would you be willing to write me a letter of recommendation? I could come to your office hours on [day], or meet on Zoom at a time that works for you. I've attached my résumé, a draft of my statement and my list of programs with deadlines.

Thank you,
[Full name]

PhD visit programs

Many universities invite prospective PhD applicants to campus in the fall to meet faculty and graduate students and learn how to apply. Most pay for travel, a hotel and meals, and some waive the application fee. Most fly-ins take applications in July and August, so apply the summer before senior year.

Every visit program is in the PhD opportunities list. Open now: Notre Dame's Our Futures Weekend (juniors, due Nov 15) and Princeton's P3 (due Mar 15).

No visit? You can still get a fee waiver. Yale waives its fee for Pell Grant recipients, and UChicago Social Sciences waives it for undergrads on need-based aid. See Applying for more.

Sample résumé and CV

Use a one-page résumé for jobs, internships and MPA/MPP applications, and an academic CV for PhD programs, predocs and research programs. Both are for a fictional QC student: copy the structure, not the content.

Download the samples

Open the Word file to edit it, or the PDF to print. Replace everything with your own details.

  • Résumé: Word · PDF
  • Academic CV: Word · PDF

Résumé vs. CV

Tips

  • Numbers make bullets believable. "4,000+ respondents" beats "large dataset."
  • Tailor the top third to the job or program.
  • Keep a master CV and cut it down for each application.
  • Drop high school once you have college experience.
  • Send a PDF named LastName_Resume.pdf.
  • Get it reviewed at QC's Center for Career Engagement and Internships (Frese 213).

Jobs with a political science degree

Few political science majors become "political scientists": that title usually means a PhD (BLS). Most work in government, law, nonprofits, media, research and business. Here are common first jobs, what employers ask for and what they pay in New York.

Pay comes from job postings in New York in 2026 and from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. BLS medians cover every experience level (New York area), so first-year pay is usually lower. Postings close; search the titles above for current ones.

Where to look

  • HireQC (Handshake). Employers looking for Queens College students.
  • NYC Jobs and StateJobsNY. City and state government. Check the civil service exam schedule early; many permanent city jobs need one.
  • USAJOBS. Federal jobs. Filter by "Recent graduates" in the two years after you finish.
  • City & State Jobs. New York politics: legislative offices, campaigns, advocacy and government affairs.
  • Idealist. Nonprofit jobs and fellowships. More tools in Job search tools.

At Queens College

  • Center for Career Engagement and Internships. Résumé reviews, mock interviews, career fairs and the FOCUS 2 career assessment. Frese Hall 213; book a career educator on QC Navigate.
  • Political Science internships. Earn credit for an internship, including full-time spring semesters in Albany with a stipend.
  • The department's brochure. Its "What kind of jobs can I get" section lists where majors go.
  • APSA's student resources. Careers in law, government, campaigns, journalism, nonprofits, business and teaching.

Get experience while you're in school. Almost every posting above asks for writing, data skills or a year of related work. An internship, a campus job or a research job with a professor counts. Not sure which job fits you? Try the prompts in Using AI the right way, then check what it says with the career center.

Scholarships and funding

Queens College has its own scholarship money, and one application each semester puts you in the running for most of it. Start there, then work with the Office of Honors and Scholarships on national awards. Every scholarship below is also in the opportunities lists with its deadline.

At Queens College

  1. Fill out the General Application every semester. One application on QC's AcademicWorks portal covers most QC Foundation scholarships, and the office says most are open to students without documentation. This fall's closes October 25, 2026; the spring cycle runs from mid-January to mid-March.
  2. Answer the supplemental questions. Some awards ask one more short question at the end, like the Ottensoser Award, which helps juniors and seniors pay graduate school application fees and test costs.
  3. Let the department know you. The Political Science department's awards have no application. Professors choose.
  4. Graduating with a 3.75 or higher? Seniors with a 3.75+ GPA and 45 QC credits get an email in the spring to be considered for the Baccalaureate Award Ceremony's named awards, including several for students headed to law school or public-interest careers. Fill out the survey in that email.
  5. Get paid for an unpaid internship. The QC Internship Stipend Fund gives $2,700 once. With a work-study award, the NYC Public Service Corps pays you to intern in government.

National awards, by year

The Office of Honors and Scholarships advises on national awards. For some, Queens College has to nominate you, and its own deadline comes before the national one, so start early.

  • Freshmen and sophomores. JK Watson Fellowship (QC nominates), Fulbright UK Summer Institutes, Critical Language Scholarship (Nov 17) and, for study abroad, Gilman.
  • Juniors. Truman, Beinecke (QC nominates), Boren and the Rangel summer program. Plan now for Rhodes, Marshall and Schwarzman: their applications are due early in senior year.
  • Seniors. Fulbright (apply through QC), Carnegie Junior Fellows (QC nominates), the Huntington Public Service Award and, for future teachers, the James Madison Fellowship.
  • Check every year. Belle Zeller (30 CUNY credits and a 3.75+ GPA), Pilsbury (first-generation), APIA Scholars and the Hispanic Scholarship Fund.

Programs that pay for housing. A summer away from home costs much less when the program houses you. With free housing and a stipend: the Hudson Institute and Hertog political studies programs ($3,000 each), Hertog's security, war and constitutional studies programs, the Publius Fellowship, and research programs like RBSI and PPIA. AEI and Hoover cover housing for their summer courses. Washington internships with housing: CHCI, CBCF, APAICS, Victory, CHLI, the Islamic Scholarship Fund, the Muslim Public Service Network, AAPD (for students with disabilities) and the Institute for Responsible Citizenship. Pre-law: USC's ASCEND and Florida State's summer program. After college, AmeriCorps NCCC, the Jesuit Volunteer Corps and the Peace Corps house you while you serve. Search every program for housing.

Study or work abroad after college. For a fully funded master's abroad, look at Rhodes and Marshall (QC must endorse you; due around October 1 of senior year), Gates Cambridge, Oxford's Clarendon, the Yenching Academy and Schwarzman in Beijing, Erasmus Mundus in Europe and DAAD in Germany. Paid teaching jobs include Fulbright English teaching assistantships, JET in Japan, TAPIF in France, language assistants in Spain and EPIK in Korea. For a service year, try Princeton in Asia, Africa or Latin America, the Luce Scholars or the Peace Corps. Every one is in All opportunities.

Muslim and Arab American students. Queens College has a large Muslim community, and several national programs are built for it. The Islamic Scholarship Fund gives $3,000–10,000 scholarships to Muslim juniors, seniors and graduate students in political science, policy, journalism and law, and runs paid congressional and newsroom internships (due Nov 1). For a summer in Washington, look at MPAC's Hill program and the Muslim Public Service Network. Closer to home, CAIR-NY in Manhattan and Emgage in Queens take students. Arab American students can apply to the Arab American Leadership Program (Dec 13) and the Arab American Institute.

Not a US citizen? Many national awards require citizenship, but not all. Most of QC's own scholarships are open to students without documentation. TheDream.US is for undocumented students, and Queens College is a partner school. The Hispanic Scholarship Fund, the Fund for Education Abroad and RBSI accept DACA recipients. Ask the Office of Honors and Scholarships about the rest.

Journalism, nonprofits and government

Not every path goes straight to graduate school. These programs pay you to report, organize or work in government, and many take students from any year.

  • Journalism. Paid newsroom internships, like POLITICO's in New York (Oct 26), and fellowships after college, like The Atlantic's (Nov 5). QC students can start CUNY's journalism master's in senior year through the Newmark 4+1. All journalism programs.
  • Nonprofits. A paid summer at a Brooklyn nonprofit through the Hope Reichbach Fellowship, a semester in Albany with NYPIRG, or a service year after college with City Year, Teach For America or NYC Civic Corps.
  • Government. The Mayor's Office, the State Attorney General, congressional offices including Rep. Grace Meng's in Queens, and federal agencies. The CIA, FBI and State Department hire 6–15 months ahead and require US citizenship.

Looking for more after college? ProFellow's free list of public service fellowships for recent graduates has dozens more, like the Carnegie Junior Fellows (QC nominates) and the CHCI and APAICS fellowships on Capitol Hill. Its full database needs a free account. Some details on ProFellow are out of date, so confirm on each program's official page.

Job search tools and AI

Most of these are free. Set up alerts once, and new openings come to you.

Free through Queens College

  • HireQC (Handshake). QC's job and internship board, including work-study jobs. Sign in with your QC credentials.
  • Résumé reviews. Book a career educator on QC Navigate, or submit your résumé for review in Handshake. The Center for Career Engagement and Internships is in Frese Hall 213.
  • Vault Career Intelligence. Profiles of employers, industries and 900 internships, plus interview guides. Create a free account.
  • The Forage. Free, self-paced job simulations from real employers, a good way to try out a field.
  • Parker Dewey micro-internships. Paid projects for real companies, usually 10 to 40 hours of work.
  • Tech Incubator at Queens College. Free Google and AWS certificates, such as Google Data Analytics; the incubator covers the cost. Apply with one short form. Its micro-internships put CUNY students on a real problem for a client company, a quick way to start a portfolio.

Job boards with email alerts

  • USAJOBS. Federal jobs. Filter by the Students or Recent Graduates hiring path, and see federal internships. Internship postings are often open only about two weeks, so turn on alerts.
  • NYC Jobs. New York City government jobs. Many city titles require a civil service exam; see the exam schedule.
  • Idealist. Nonprofit and public-interest jobs, with daily email alerts.
  • PREDOC.org. Research jobs before a PhD. Sign up on the page to get postings in your field by email.
  • LinkedIn job alerts. Up to 20 alerts, sent daily or weekly. Its AI job search lets you describe the job you want in your own words.

More résumé help

  • Headless Headhunter. A recruiter's free résumé guide, templates and résumé review episodes. He writes for corporate jobs, so take his advice with a grain of salt for government, nonprofit and academic applications. It's most useful if you pair political science with something like data, business or tech.
  • Samples on this site. A one-page résumé and an academic CV, and a law school résumé.

AI that helps without writing for you

For profiles, prompts, interview practice and what not to do, see Using AI the right way.

CUNY licenses one generative AI tool for all students: Microsoft Copilot Chat. Sign in with your CUNY Login email, not a personal Microsoft account. That way your chats fall under Microsoft's enterprise data protection and aren't used to train its models. Even so, CUNY's AI guidance says not to share sensitive or identifiable information with any AI tool.

  • Read a posting. Paste in a job or program description and ask for a checklist of what it requires and what you need to prepare.
  • Track deadlines. Ask it to turn your list of programs into a table of deadlines, materials and recommenders, then copy it into Excel.
  • Practice interviews. Ask it to play the interviewer for a specific internship, one question at a time. Answer out loud, then ask for feedback.
  • Prepare for a conversation. Ask it to summarize an organization's recent work before an interview or networking call, then check those facts on the organization's own site.
  • Job-search apps. Apps like Jobright match you to postings and track your applications. Most have a free plan, and many software companies give students a discount: sign up with your CUNY email and look for student pricing before you pay.

Don't let it write your applications. The rule from Statements, help and AI applies here too. Some programs set limits: MIT Blueprint Labs caps code samples at 50% AI-assisted. Many job tools, including LinkedIn Premium, offer to write cover letters or "tailor" your résumé for you; skip those features.

Using AI the right way

AI is a good helper in a job search: it can sharpen your profiles, find openings, check your grammar and quiz you before an interview. It is a bad ghostwriter. Readers notice AI-written applications, and some programs disqualify them.

Where it helps

  • Your LinkedIn and Handshake profiles. Paste in your headline and About section and ask what is vague or missing, then fix it in your own words. LinkedIn's built-in writing help needs Premium; Microsoft's free module shows how to do it with Copilot. Handshake has its own AI features, and a complete profile shows up in more employer searches.
  • Finding jobs. Describe the job you want in plain words in Handshake or LinkedIn's AI job search, and ask AI which job titles to search for.
  • Proofreading. Give it your draft and ask it to point out grammar mistakes, unclear sentences and weak verbs, not to rewrite it. Harvard's career office shows how.
  • Fixing your résumé. Paste a job posting and your résumé and ask which skills the posting wants that you haven't shown, then add only what's true. Video: Tailor your résumé using Gemini (Google, 5 minutes).
  • Practicing interviews. Ask it to play the interviewer, one question at a time, and to give feedback on each answer. Videos: Practice interviewing with Gemini Live (Google, 3 minutes) and Prepare for a job interview with AI (UNLV Career Services, 12 minutes). Free practice tools: Interviews by AI (3 questions a month) and Yoodli (5 practice rounds). For a real person, book a mock interview at the career center.

Not sure what you want to do?

Tell it who you are and what you like, and it can point you to jobs you haven't heard of. Then check what it says against real sources, like O*NET, the career center and people who do the job. Columbia's career center has more ideas.

Prompts to try

I'm a [year] political science major at Queens College in New York. I like [classes or topics], I'm good at [skills], and I care about [issues]. I don't know what job I want. Suggest 10 entry-level job titles that fit me, what each one does day to day, and what I'd need to get hired.

For [job title], what does a normal day look like, what do people like and dislike about it, and what could I do this semester to find out if it's for me?

Here is a job posting: [paste]. Here is my experience: [paste]. What am I missing, and how could I build it in the next six months?

Act as an interviewer for [job] at [organization]. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, then tell me what was strong and what to improve.

Don't let it write for you. In a Robert Half survey (March 2026), 67% of HR leaders said AI-generated applications were slowing hiring. Some applications say it outright: the Commonpoint Data & Insights Fellowship asks for answers in your own words and may disqualify ones that look AI-generated, and 45% of the law schools in a Kaplan survey ban using AI to write the admissions essay. Skip tools that feed you answers during a real interview; employers prohibit them.

Remember: you can coast through a degree using AI all through college, and maybe even graduate, but no one will hire you if you're not competent or useful.

Mohamed Aljahmi

Use Copilot Chat with your CUNY Login: CUNY licenses it for students, and your chats aren't used to train Microsoft's models. They aren't private from CUNY's IT staff (Microsoft), so don't paste in anything sensitive.

Building a network

Many jobs and internships come through people you know, and you're in New York City, which has more networking events than you could ever go to.

  • Ask your professors. Tell them the field you're curious about, and ask whether they know anyone you could talk to.
  • Use the career center. The Center for Career Engagement and Internships runs workshops and events and a career and internship fair where employers recruit.
  • Go to events. Look for talks, panels and mixers at CUNY, nonprofits, think tanks and city agencies; many are free. Introduce yourself, ask one good question, and follow up by email.

This is all general advice, so don't feel pressured. I know it's overwhelming. But if you put in your best effort and explore what you really like, you can find a job in that sector, whatever you want it to be, or get into law school or graduate school. Just take your time and put effort into your classwork, your applications and networking. Don't be afraid: people are usually nice and will help you. You just have to make it easy for them!

Mohamed Aljahmi

What law school takes

Admissions weigh two numbers most, your LSAT score and your GPA, then your personal statement, letters and résumé. Your major does not need to be pre-law or political science. Not sure what kind of law? See Fields of law.

One application cycle (LSAC's steps)

  1. Spring before you apply. Request the LSAC fee waiver if you might qualify, at least 6 months before your first LSAT.
  2. June or September–October. Take the LSAT. Many schools want a score by November or December.
  3. Summer. Draft the personal statement; ask 2–3 professors or supervisors for letters.
  4. 6–8 weeks before your first deadline. Register for CAS, which sends your transcripts and letters to every school.
  5. September–December. Submit applications. Earlier is better at schools that admit on a rolling basis.
  6. Winter–spring. Decisions and scholarship offers. QC's pre-law advisor helps you compare and negotiate.

The LSAT today

Since August 2024 there are no logic games: two scored Logical Reasoning sections, one scored Reading Comprehension section and one unscored section, scored 120–180, plus a separate Argumentative Writing sample (LSAC). Many schools also accept the GRE.

Time off is normal

  • 86% of Harvard Law's Class of 2029 spent at least a year out of college (HLS)
  • ~1 in 3 of 2024 first-year law students nationally came straight from college (LSAC)

Your timeline

Freshman and sophomore years are for GPA, professors and a first internship. The LSAT comes junior summer at the earliest.

Opportunities

Pre-law programs, legal and city internships, and scholarships for law school, soonest deadline first.

Sorted by next deadline. Dates are this cycle's where posted; otherwise they are last cycle's, which are usually close. Confirm on the official page.

Ottensoser Award for Higher Education

Deadline: Oct 25, 2026 · in the General Application

Juniors and seniors · QC scholarship · graduate school application costs

QC Scholarships, General Application

Deadline: Oct 25, 2026 · spring cycle mid-Jan to mid-Mar

All years · QC Foundation scholarships · one application, every semester

One general application on QC's AcademicWorks portal puts you in the running for most of the college's donor scholarships, based on merit, need, major or class year. Fall applications pay for the spring term, and spring applications pay for the fall. A few awards add a short supplemental question at the end.

  • Who: Matriculated QC students with a QC email, including second-degree students. The office says most awards are open to students without documentation
  • For political science: Minister Jason Peck ($500; preference for political science majors and minors), Sig and Mary Hecht (financial need and a 3.0+ GPA in a social science), Swimmer (preference for students interested in law) and Brownstein/McDermott ($5,000; political theory counts; 30+ credits and a 3.5+ GPA)
  • Tip: Apply every semester. The office suggests listing a reference (email them first) and any community service

When: Each semester · through a campus faculty coordinator

Sophomores, juniors and seniors · CUNY · government internships for credit

  • Start: Ask the Political Science department who coordinates it at Queens College

Fordham Law IDEAL pre-law program

Deadline: Jan 30, 2027 · opens in December
Opens: Dec 2026

Sophomores and juniors · Fordham Law, Manhattan, and online · 10 weeks each summer, June to early August

A free two-summer pre-law program at Fordham Law for New York City-area college students. Summer I (apply as a sophomore) introduces law school through Fordham's online Pre-Law Institute, visits to law firms and the DA's office, and mentoring. Summer II (apply as a junior) is a 10-week LSAT boot camp with a judicial internship and help with law school applications. Online information sessions: Nov 2 and Nov 6, 2026.

  • Who: Full-time sophomores (no more than 90 credits by June 1, 2027) or juniors (no more than 105 credits and a 3.5+ GPA) at four-year colleges, with a strong interest in law
  • Pay: Free, with some meals and a modest stipend; no housing or travel to campus
  • Note: You can't hold another job or internship during the summer

A free two-summer program for sophomores. Summer I has law mini-courses, legal writing and visits to firms and agencies; junior year brings a paid LSAT course and mentors; Summer II is an application boot camp and a paid legal internship. UVA picks 8 to 12 scholars a year.

  • Apply: Online application, a résumé, unofficial transcripts and two letters; no interview

BU Law Summer Pre-Law Academy

Deadline: ~Feb 26 · est. · opens Dec 16
Opens: Dec 16

Juniors, seniors and recent grads · Boston University School of Law · 4 weeks in residence, June 7–July 1, 2027

Free law school classes taught Socratic-style, case briefing, a group "client" project, LSAT prep and help with your personal statement and résumé. Priority goes to students within a year of starting law school, mostly rising seniors.

  • Who: Current undergraduates and college graduates, with priority for those within a year of starting law school
  • Pay: Free to apply and attend. Travel to Boston, housing and many meals are covered, plus a $1,500 stipend when you finish
  • Apply: Application form, a one- to two-page statement of interest, a résumé and an unofficial transcript; no letters. BU's page says Feb 26, 2026, which looks like a typo for 2027

FSU Law Donald J. Weidner Summer for Undergraduates Program

Deadline: Mar 1, 2027 · no application fee
Opens: Nov 1

Freshmen, sophomores and juniors · Florida State University, Tallahassee · June 2–29, 2027

Mock first-year law classes, legal writing workshops, admissions coaching and court visits. It has run since 1992.

  • Who: Students at two- or four-year colleges in any major who won't have a bachelor's degree before the program starts
  • Covered: Free campus apartment housing and a meal card; you pay travel

Duke PreLaw Fellowship Program

Deadline: ~Early March · est. · applications open January 2027
Opens: January 2027

Freshmen and sophomores · Duke Law, Durham, N.C. · 4 weeks in residence in early summer (2026: May 31–June 26)

A free four-week summer program at Duke Law: mini-courses taught by Duke Law faculty, LSAT information, visits to other law schools and law firms, and courthouse tours. Each cohort has 24 Fellows.

  • Who: Students finishing their freshman or sophomore year at a four-year, technical or community college, especially first-generation and low-income students. Colleges in the Southeast are encouraged, but students from other regions can apply
  • Pay: All programming, room and board, books and course packets are free, plus a $1,000 stipend. Travel isn't mentioned
  • Apply: Finalists may get a Zoom interview. Questions: dlpp@law.duke.edu

Minnesota Pre-Law Scholars (MPLS) Program

Deadline: Mar 15 · last cycle · opens late January
Opens: Late January

Juniors, seniors and recent grads · Online · 11 weeks of evening LSAT classes, June to mid-August

A free online LSAT course from the University of Minnesota Law School, three evenings a week, with admissions and career sessions. A second track offers only the admissions and career sessions.

  • Who: Students and graduates of any college with a 3.5 GPA who will apply to law school in the next cycle
  • Cost: Free, with study materials. Plan on 15 to 20 hours of study a week
  • Apply: Application, unofficial transcripts, a statement of interest and a practice or official LSAT score

Pre-Law Summer Institute for American Indians and Alaska Natives

Deadline: Mar 20 · last cycle

Seniors and recent grads · American Indian Law Center, UNM School of Law, Albuquerque · 8 weeks, late May to late July

An intensive two-month program that copies a first semester of law school: Federal Indian Law, first-year courses, legal writing and moot court.

  • Who: American Indian and Alaska Native students with proof of tribal membership or descent, who have taken the LSAT, will finish college by May and have applied to an ABA law school
  • Cost: No charge to attend; you pay travel and living costs. Students ask their tribes for help, and PLSI helps if a tribe can't

USC Gould ASCEND Pre-Law Summer Institute

Deadline: Mar 31, 2027 · opens Feb 1
Opens: Feb 1

Freshmen, sophomores and juniors · USC, Los Angeles · 3 weeks, July 11–31, 2027

A free three-week residential preview of law school, with LSAT prep, court and law firm visits, and mentors.

  • Covered: Instruction, housing and meals, up to $450 for a round-trip flight, and $500 toward LSAT costs when you finish

New York Law School Summer Pre-Law Program

Deadline: Apr 10 · last cycle

Sophomores · New York Law School, Manhattan · 4 weeks in each of two summers, 4 days a week

  • Who: Rising juniors from NYC or New York State. NYLS works with partner colleges to find candidates, but anyone can fill out the application
  • Cost: Not stated on the official page

University at Buffalo Discover Law Undergraduate Scholars Program

Deadline: Apr 13 · last cycle · 2027 dates early next year

Freshmen and sophomores · UB School of Law (SUNY), Buffalo, N.Y. · 4 weeks in residence, late May to late June

A free four-week preview of law school with classes taught by UB Law faculty, weekdays 9 to 4:30, for first-generation, Pell-eligible and economically disadvantaged students.

  • Who: Students finishing their freshman or sophomore year; first-generation, Pell-eligible, veterans or economically disadvantaged. A 3.0 GPA helps. Western, central and eastern New York residents get first consideration, but others are encouraged to apply
  • Cost: Free. Campus housing (required) and most meals are covered; you pay Saturday meals and travel
  • Apply: Personal statement, official transcript, one to three letters and a résumé

Columbia Law LEAD

Deadline: June 15, 2027 · opens Apr 15
Opens: Apr 15

Juniors and seniors · 2-year deferral

Admitted now, enroll after two years of work. LSAT or GRE by June 15.

  • Cost: The $85 application fee is waived; you pay for the LSAT or GRE and CAS

CUNY Law Pipeline to Justice

Deadline: July 1, 2027 · opens late winter
Opens: Late winter

Seniors and recent grads · Evenings, September–May

LSAT and skills program for applicants from underrepresented communities, including those denied by CUNY Law.

  • Who: Needs an LSAT score from the past 5 years; in person only, at CUNY Law in Long Island City
  • Cost: $60 application fee plus a one-time program fee (amount not posted), and you pay for the January and February LSATs. No scholarships or aid; finishing the program waives CUNY Law's seat deposit if you enroll there

Harvard Law Junior Deferral Program

Opens: May 1

Juniors · No application fee

If admitted, work at least 2 years, then enroll. LSAT or GRE by July 1.

  • Cost: No application fee and no CAS needed; you pay for the LSAT or GRE

A free 12-week online LSAT course with practice tests, plus a day of mock classes and meetings with deans and admissions staff. About 40 students per cohort.

  • Who: Anyone planning to take the LSAT in the next two years
  • Cost: Free (funded by an LSAC grant); you pay travel for the Saturday visit
  • Catch: You must include Widener Law Commonwealth among the law schools you apply to

CLEO ASAP

When: Summer 2027 · interest form open
Opens: Interest form open

Juniors, seniors and recent grads · Two-day summer workshop · last cycle included Aug 7–8 at New York Law School

  • Who: Juniors through postgrads; 2.7 GPA
  • Cost: $30 application fee and a $50 seat deposit if you're accepted (2026). Travel, housing and meals aren't mentioned

Drexel Kline Law Sheller Law School Pipeline Program

When: April · opens Apr 1, 2027
Opens: Apr 1, 2027

Sophomores, juniors, seniors and recent grads · Online, weekdays 9 to noon, 3 weeks in July · optional in-person days in Philadelphia

A free, mostly online program you can do from Queens: LSAT prep, help with the law school application, mentors, briefing cases, public speaking and community lawyering.

  • Who: Students with at least one year done at a two- or four-year college, recent graduates or postgraduates, with a 3.0 GPA, who are underrepresented in law, first-generation or have faced hardship. You must attend every required session

Suffolk Law Summer Pre-Law Achievers Network

Two non-credit mini-courses taught by law professors (a first-year subject and legal writing), court visits, meetings with Boston lawyers and an application workshop with one-on-one help. No LSAT course.

  • Who: Students in a bachelor's program or graduates of the last year or two who plan to start law school in 2028 or 2029, with a 3.0 GPA; first-generation, low-income or underrepresented
  • Cost: Free, with free dorm housing and breakfast and lunch on program days; you pay dinners and weekend meals. Travel isn't mentioned

LSAT prep, mentoring and a weeklong residential program.

Start here

This path collects the free pre-law programs, NYC internships, scholarships and LSAT logistics a QC political science major needs, whether you apply senior year or five years from now.

Three ground rules

  • The best pre-law programs are free. The LSAC fee waiver, LSAC Plus and most pipeline programs cost nothing. Be skeptical of paid "pre-law institutes."
  • Deadlines move every year. Confirm on the official page before you plan around a date.
  • Taking time off is normal. Most law students did not go straight from college.

Fields of law

Law is many different jobs. You don't have to pick a field before law school, but knowing them helps you choose internships and explain your interest in your personal statement. For a paragraph on each, see LSAC's Fields of Law; for more depth, read the guide linked under each field below. Most were written by law school career offices.

  • Criminal law. Prosecutors charge and try crimes for the government; defense lawyers, often public defenders, represent the people accused. Read: UCLA Law's guides to public defense and prosecution. Try it: the Queens DA or the city's defender offices.
  • Civil rights and civil liberties. Lawyers who use lawsuits, policy advocacy and government enforcement to protect equal treatment, voting, speech and other rights. Read: Civil Rights/Civil Liberties (Georgetown Law). Try it: the ACLU, LatinoJustice LAWbound or the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
  • Immigration law. Lawyers who help people get visas, green cards, citizenship or asylum, and defend people facing deportation. A second language helps. Read: Immigration Law Career Guide (Harvard Law). Try it: Immigrant Justice Corps after college.
  • Public interest and legal aid. Nonprofit lawyers who represent low-income clients for free in problems like evictions, debt, public benefits and consumer fraud. Read: Legal Services Career Guide (Harvard Law, 2013). Try it: the Hope Reichbach Fellowship at a Brooklyn nonprofit.
  • Government. City, state and federal lawyers who advise agencies, enforce and defend laws in court, and draft legislation and regulations. Read: State and Local Government Career Guide (Harvard Law), which profiles the NYC Law Department. Try it: the State Attorney General or the Mayor's Office.
  • Corporate and business law. Lawyers who help companies form, raise money, merge and make deals, mostly drafting and negotiating contracts rather than going to court. Most start at large firms. Read: Careers in Transactional Law (Georgetown Law, 2021). Try it: the SEO Law Fellowship.
  • Civil litigation. Lawyers who handle non-criminal lawsuits between people, companies or governments, from gathering evidence through settlement, trial and appeal. Read: Civil Litigation (University of Baltimore Law). Try it: a judge's chambers through the Sotomayor internship or the state courts.
  • International law and human rights. Lawyers working on the rules between countries and on human rights, for governments, the UN, international courts, nonprofits or global firms. Read: Careers in Public International Law and Human Rights (UCLA Law, 2019). Try it: the Council on Foreign Relations or, after college, the Carnegie Junior Fellows.
  • Environmental and energy law. Lawyers working on pollution, climate, land, water and energy rules for agencies, advocacy groups, companies or utilities. Read: Different Career Paths in Environmental Law (American Bar Association, 2020). Try it: the Udall Scholarship.
  • Labor and employment law. Lawyers who handle unions, wages, discrimination and firing, for workers, unions, employers or agencies like the NLRB and EEOC. Read: Employment/Labor Law (Georgetown Law).
  • Family law. Lawyers who handle divorce, custody, child support, adoption, domestic violence and child-welfare cases. Read: Constructing a Legal Education for a Career in Family Law (NYU Law), which names New York City employers. Try it: the city's defender offices, several of which have family defense practices.
  • Intellectual property, technology and privacy. Lawyers who protect inventions, brands and creative work, and advise on technology, data privacy and cybersecurity. Patent work needs a science or engineering background; trademark, copyright and privacy work doesn't. Read: Intellectual Property Law (Georgetown Law).
  • Health law. Lawyers who advise hospitals, insurers, drug companies, patients and agencies on health regulation, fraud, privacy and access to care. Read: Health Law (Georgetown Law).
  • Tax law. Lawyers who plan deals around tax rules and handle audits and disputes, at firms, accounting firms, companies or the government. Read: An Introduction to Tax Careers for J.D.s (American Bar Association, 2019).
  • Election law and voting rights. Lawyers who work on voting rights, redistricting, campaign finance and how elections are run, for campaigns, parties, nonprofits and election agencies. Close to political science. Read: Polling Election Lawyers (Harvard Law's Center on the Legal Profession, 2022). Try it: the Brennan Center or Emgage in Queens.

QC and CUNY resources

Start with QC's pre-law advisor, who sits in the Academic Advising Center, and the Legal Studies minor, whose three required courses also count toward the major.

  • Clubs. The pre-law page mentions a Legal Studies Club that meets monthly. Model UN, the Political Science Club and QC Future 1Ls are listed on UKnighted. The Political Science Club lists mock trials among its activities, and PSCI 288 covers mock trial and moot court.
  • A warning about research programs. The CUNY Pipeline Program, Leadership Alliance and Big Ten SROP exclude students headed to law school.
  • Scholarships. Fill out QC's General Application every semester; one award in it, the Swimmer Scholarship, gives preference to students interested in law. The Political Science department's Morrison Scholarship favors seniors headed to law school, and graduating seniors with a 3.75+ GPA are considered for law fellowships at the Baccalaureate ceremony. Muslim seniors headed to law school can apply to the Islamic Scholarship Fund's law track. More in Scholarships and funding.
  • Government and nonprofit work. Paid internships with the State Attorney General, the Mayor's Office, the Supreme Court and the ACLU, plus more in Journalism, nonprofits and government.
  • Jobs, letters and networking. HireQC (Handshake), résumé help, free certificates, job boards and CUNY's AI tool are in Job search tools and AI. See also Recommendation letters and Building a network.

Research as a pre-law student

Research isn't required for law school, but it builds what admissions reads for: careful writing and a professor who knows your work.

  • Honors in the Social Sciences. A thesis on bail, sentencing or voting rights gives you a writing sample and a close mentor. 3.3 GPA to start.
  • Methods courses. PSCI 200 and an intro statistics course, such as PSYCH 107 or DATA 205, teach you to read the empirical studies courts and advocates cite.
  • Faculty research work. Email a professor whose work on courts, policing, immigration or rights interests you, and offer a set number of hours a week.
  • Data work at legal organizations. Some defender offices, DA offices and legal aid groups take interns who clean data and summarize case records.
  • Present it. The Borough of Queens Undergraduate Research Symposium takes projects from every field each spring.
  • Split between law and a PhD? Research serves both. See the graduate school path for PhD programs.

LSAT and fees

One LSAT plus CAS and six school reports costs about $740 before prep. If money is tight, apply for the LSAC fee waiver at least six months before your first test.

2026–27 test dates (LSAC)

What it costs (LSAC)

The LSAC fee waiver. Based on income and assets. Income limits run from 150% to 300% of the federal poverty guidelines, depending on the tier and whether your parents' income counts. Tier 1 covers 2 LSATs with Writing and Score Preview, CAS, 6 law school reports and LawHub Advantage; Tier 2 covers 1 LSAT, CAS, 3 reports and LawHub Advantage. The LSAT and CAS benefits last two years; LawHub Advantage lasts one year. US citizens, permanent residents, DACA recipients, asylum seekers and TPS holders are eligible. Apply, and ask each law school whether it waives its own fee too.

Free and low-cost prep

  • LawHub. The free tier includes full official practice tests. Khan Academy's free LSAT course ended June 30, 2024; its content moved here.
  • LawHub Advantage. The paid tier with many more official tests, included with LSAC Plus and the fee waiver.
  • AccessLex LexPreLaw. Kaplan LSAT prep, admissions counseling and financial help for 150 underrepresented applicants a year. You need an LSAT score already, at or below the 25th percentile. The 2027 application opens in March.
  • The GRE option. ETS's list includes NYU, Columbia, Fordham, Brooklyn, Cardozo, St. John's, Pace, Hofstra and Touro. CUNY Law is not on it.

Gap years

A paid job between college and law school is the norm at top schools, and the work you do can become the story in your personal statement.

Using the time well. Keep in touch with one or two professors so they can still write letters. Take the LSAT while you are working rather than cramming in the fall you apply.

Sample law school résumé

A law school résumé is a job résumé with three differences: list your hours per week for jobs held during school, add an interests line, and skip the objective.

Download the samples

Open the Word file to edit it, or the PDF to print. Replace everything with your own details.

  • Law résumé: Word · PDF

Rules from admissions offices

  • 1–2 pages. Trim to one if the second page is less than half full (Maryland Carey Law).
  • One page where asked. Wisconsin's advisors name Yale and Northwestern (UW–Madison pre-law).
  • Hours per week for every job held during school. It explains a GPA earned while working.
  • An interests line brings the application to life.
  • No high school, no objective, no fancy fonts.

Before you send it

  • Make every date match your application form.
  • Keep one format: title, organization, city, dates, hours.
  • Ask QC Pre-Law Advising to review it.
